text: The query is written. Now it's time to open Power BI Desktop and bring that data in -- and the first real decision is which connection mode to use.

Power BI offers Import or DirectQuery. This report uses Import. The dataset is tiny -- four rows at most, one per product category, for a single quarter. And the stakeholder only needs to pull this up during a meeting, not watch live-updating numbers. Import gives faster visuals and lets you build and test the report without the database needing to be reachable every time you open the file.

Connecting is Get Data, SQL Server, enter the server name, and open Advanced options. Paste the entire Lesson 3 query into the SQL statement box and click OK. Power BI runs it against AdventureWorks2012 and previews exactly the three columns from the select list. Choose Transform Data, not Load, so there's a chance to check things before anything lands in the model.

Three checks belong in Power Query before loading. Column names -- CategoryName, TotalSalesAmount, OrderCount should already be clean, since the query aliased them, but confirm it. Data types -- TotalSalesAmount should be a decimal number, OrderCount a whole number; SQL Server's money type sometimes imports as text if the connector guesses wrong, and that mistake is much easier to catch here than after a DAX measure quietly returns blank. And a row count sanity check -- this should load four rows or fewer, one per AdventureWorks2012 product category. More than four means something upstream is wrong.

One more small thing worth doing: rename the query itself from the generic default to something like CategoryPerformanceSnapshot. That name shows up in the data model, and it should describe what the data actually is.
With the data checked and loaded, next lesson we sketch the report page layout -- which visuals go where, and why planning that first beats dragging things onto the canvas at random.
